title: How the Space Station Flies Over a Hurricane
description: The International Space Station captures the immense scale and power of hurricanes from low Earth orbit. These storms release heat at a rate two hundred times the world's electricity generation.

shots.narration: From space, a hurricane is calm in the middle and terrifying everywhere else.
This is the eye of Hurricane Milton, a quiet center typically thirty to sixty-five kilometres wide.
The strongest winds blow in the wall around this eye, where speeds can exceed two hundred fifty kilometres per hour.
A large hurricane can be more than one thousand kilometres across, dominating the curve of the Earth.
The International Space Station travels so fast it crosses an entire storm system in about two minutes.
A mature hurricane releases heat at a rate about two hundred times the world's total electricity generation.
North of the equator, these massive cloud bands spin anticlockwise, while southern storms rotate clockwise.
From thirty-five thousand eight hundred kilometres up, GOES weather satellites image these storms every thirty seconds.
The textured cloud tops hide the chaos below, where the eyewall winds are at their most violent.
